opus-5.5.text:
Well, it came about quite naturally, really. The China Computer Federation was putting together its encyclopedia-style entries on emerging fields, and embodied intelligence had become one of those terms everyone was using but few people agreed on. Some people meant humanoid robots, some meant large models plus a body, some meant reinforcement learning in simulation. So there was a real need for someone to sit down and write a definition that the community could point to.

Cewu and I have known each other for a long time. We're both working on the problem from somewhat different angles. His group has done a lot on manipulation, perception of human-object interaction, and grasping. My own work has come from 3D vision, simulation, synthetic data, and generalizable manipulation. Writing it together let us cover more of the landscape than either of us would alone, and it kept the entry from becoming one lab's worldview.

For me, the deeper motivation was to stake out what I think the field actually is. Embodied intelligence isn't just "put a model on a robot." The core idea is that intelligence comes from an agent with a body interacting with the physical world: perceiving, acting, getting feedback, and learning from that loop. That distinguishes it from internet AI, which learns from static data people have already produced. Once you frame it that way, the key bottlenecks become clear: data, generalization, and the gap between simulation and reality. We wanted the entry to reflect that, so newcomers—students, investors, policymakers—start from a correct mental model rather than the hype.

So in a sense it was a bit of community service, and a bit of trying to set the agenda for the next several years.

r001.rationale: The candidate says coauthoring let them cover more perspectives and avoid one lab’s worldview, but does not say Lu invited He or that Lu was concerned a sole-authored definition would reflect only his own perspective.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the starting point was a bit of a vacuum. When the China Computer Federation was putting together its encyclopedia entries, "embodied intelligence" was a term everyone had started using, but almost no one agreed on what it actually meant. Some people treated it as a synonym for humanoid robots, some as a rebrand of classical robotics, some as "large models with a body attached." Cewu and I both felt that if the field was going to grow in China, there needed to be at least one carefully written reference that a student or an investor or a government official could point to and say, this is roughly what the community means.

Why the two of us together? We come at the problem from different ends. Cewu's background is deeper in computer vision and human-object interaction, in understanding how humans actually use their hands and bodies, and he has thought a lot about data and benchmarks for manipulation. My own path went through 3D vision and point clouds, and then increasingly toward generalizable policies, simulation, and getting robots to act in the open world. If either of us had written the entry alone, it would have leaned toward our own biases. Writing it together forced us to argue through the parts where we disagreed, and I think the entry is better for that.

The core thing we wanted to get across is that embodied intelligence is not primarily about the hardware form. It is about an agent that perceives, acts, and learns through interaction with a physical environment, where the body and the environment are part of the learning loop rather than an afterthought. Once you frame it that way, a lot of things fall into place: why simulation and real data both matter, why generalization is the hard problem rather than any single task, and why language models are a useful component but not the whole story.

We also wanted to be honest about what we don't know yet. An encyclopedia entry tends to sound authoritative, but this is a field that is moving month to month. So we tried to separate the parts that are fairly settled, like the basic perception-action loop and the role of learning, from the parts that are still open bets, like which data strategy will scale. I hope people read it as a map of a moving frontier, not a finished definition.

astra-6.text: Embodied intelligence brings together several areas—perception, learning, decision-making, and interaction with the physical world. Cewu and I could bring complementary perspectives to the entry. The aim was to give readers a clear, shared starting point: what embodied intelligence means, why embodiment matters, and how the different research directions fit together.

sol-6.1.text: Cewu and I share an interest in embodied intelligence, but we approach it from somewhat different angles. Writing the entry together was a way to bring those perspectives into one coherent explanation. We wanted to clarify the central idea: intelligence isn’t just processing information in isolation. It develops through an agent’s perception, actions, and interaction with its environment. That connection is especially important when we talk about robots operating in the real world.
